title: Birbal and the Persian Scholar
summary: An arrogant linguist challenges Akbar's court to discover his true mother tongue. Birbal solves the puzzle in the middle of the night.
full_text:
A renowned scholar and polyglot named Mirza Behram arrived at the imperial court of Emperor Akbar from Central Asia. He was a master of languages, speaking Persian, Arabic, Sanskrit, Turkish, French, Hindi, Tamil, and Bengali with flawless pronunciation, perfect grammar, and authentic native accents.

Standing proudly in the Diwan-i-Khas, the scholar challenged the Emperor: 'Your Majesty, I have traveled across the world. No king or scholar has ever been able to determine which of these tongues is my true native mother tongue! I challenge your famous Navratnas: discover my mother tongue within twenty-four hours, or admit that my intellect surpasses all of Hindustan!'

Akbar summoned his greatest scholars. For hours, they engaged Mirza Behram in debate. He spoke Sanskrit like a Varanasi pandit; he spoke Persian like an Isfahan poet; he spoke Tamil like a Madurai scholar. By evening, the imperial scholars were exhausted and utterly defeated.

Akbar turned to Birbal: 'Birbal, the honor of our court is at stake. Can you find the scholar's mother tongue?'

'Give me until tomorrow morning, Sire,' Birbal replied with a calm bow.

That night, Mirza Behram was housed in a luxurious guest pavilion within the palace gardens. After a heavy feast, the scholar fell into a deep, peaceful slumber.

Around two o'clock in the morning, when the palace was shrouded in complete darkness, Birbal silently entered the scholar's bedroom carrying a long peacock feather and a cup of ice-cold water.

Birbal leaned over the sleeping scholar, dipped the tip of the feather into the freezing water, and gently tickled the scholar's ear and nose!

Mirza Behram stirred and muttered in his sleep. Birbal tickled his ear again, more vigorously.

Startled from deep sleep by the freezing tickle, the scholar leaped up in bed and shouted furiously in the dark: 'Aare koun hai re? Kahe hamri neend kharab karat ho? Bhag yahan se!' (Who is it? Why are you ruining my sleep? Get out of here!)

Birbal stepped out from the shadows, bowed politely, and said: 'Good night, noble scholar. Forgive the intrusion!'

The next morning in the imperial court, Mirza Behram stood proudly before Akbar: 'Has anyone discovered my native tongue?'

Birbal stepped forward: 'Your native mother tongue is Bhojpuri, spoken in the eastern plains of Hindustan!'

The scholar's jaw dropped. He blushed deeply and bowed to the floor: 'It is true! Bhojpuri is the tongue my mother spoke to me in childhood. But how did you uncover it when I spoke only refined Persian and Arabic in this court?'

Birbal smiled: 'A man may learn a dozen languages to display his learning when his mind is alert. But when a man is startled in the dark or struck by sudden pain, all pretense falls away, and he invariably cries out in his mother tongue!'

Akbar and the courtiers applauded Birbal's brilliant practical psychology.
moral: A man may master a hundred foreign tongues, but in sudden pain, his true mother tongue cries out.
